card.hook: Twelve columns, five passageways and a bronze goddess driving four horses, and by late morning half the world seems to be standing in front of them with a phone. Get there early and you can have the whole scene to yourself.
card.stand_here: Stand in Pariser Platz, on the east side of the square, facing west toward the gate. You'll get the front of the gate with the six columns and the Quadriga centred above, and the cobbles in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits the whole gate with the square in front of it. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the Quadriga and the column details. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of cobbles and sky, and keep the gate in the middle so the edges don't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the centre of the gate up with the middle vertical line and hold the phone level so the columns don't lean.
card.best_time: Sunrise is best: the square is quiet and the sun is behind you. From late morning it gets very crowded. The floodlighting is switched off from 26 October to early December 2026 for renewal, so night shots may not work then.
card.selfie_here: Pariser Platz, on the east side of the gate, is the daytime selfie square. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the gate over your shoulder (check the angle on the spot). For a quieter backdrop, try the left (north) side of the square, in front of the Akademie der Künste and the DZ Bank buildings.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Straße des 17. Juni just west of the gate, looking back east, while you stand in front of the gate with the Quadriga seen from behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The gate stands in an open public square, but check the official site before you go for events, closures or restrictions.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the columns are dead straight and not a single stranger is in the frame. Bonus points if you can count all four horses.
card.good_to_know: The gate was built between 1788 and 1791 for King Frederick William II of Prussia, and Carl Gotthard Langhans was the architect. The Quadriga on top was made by the sculptor Johann Gottfried Schadow. During the Cold War the Berlin Wall blocked the gateway, and since 1990 the gate has stood as a symbol of unity and peace.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Pariser Platz, on the east side of the square, facing west toward the gate. You'll get the front of the gate with the six columns and the Quadriga centred above, and the cobbles in front of you.

card.hook: Picture old stone columns with a modern glass dome perched right behind them. That mix is the whole reason this view works, and the wide lawn keeps everything else out of your way.
card.stand_here: Stand on Platz der Republik, on the open lawn directly in front of the west façade. The Reichstag lies to the east of you, so face east and you'll get the columns with the glass dome rising behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole west front with the dome behind it. If you're close and the building won't fit, drop to 0.5x. For the dome or the words above the entrance, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the entrance on the centre line so the columns look straight, then tap the building and nudge it a little darker to keep the sky blue.
card.best_time: Afternoon is the pick, when the sun is behind you as you face the building, according to one traveller review. Go early if you want fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the grass in front of the main façade, where people sit and rest in the meadow. Use the front camera (try 0.5x) and hold it a bit low, so the whole Reichstag fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand among the rows of stelae at the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe, across the street, and shoot back toward the Reichstag while you stand on the lawn.
card.rules_and_safety: The lawn was reported muddy and under groundworks in June 2025, so check its condition on the day. The dome and rooftop terrace need advance online registration, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in and catch the words "Dem deutschen Volke" above the main entrance without cutting off a single letter.
card.good_to_know: The Reichstag is the seat of Germany's Bundestag. It was built between 1884 and 1894 to designs by Paul Wallot. Norman Foster redesigned it between 1995 and 1999, and it was handed over for parliament use in April 1999. The inscription above the entrance was added in 1916.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Platz der Republik, on the open lawn directly in front of the west façade. The Reichstag lies to the east of you, so face east and you'll get the columns with the glass dome rising behind.

card.hook: A little guardhouse with sandbags sits in the middle of a busy Berlin crossroads while cars sweep past it like it's nothing. That's Checkpoint Charlie, and the booth, the sign and the street tell the whole story in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the replica booth in the middle of Friedrichstraße and Zimmerstraße. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so you can walk straight up to it. Face the guardhouse so you get its 'You are leaving the American Sector' sign, the sandbags and the flags.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the booth, sign and street in one go. If the pavement is packed and you can't step back, zoom 0.5x helps, but keep the booth away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Zoom 2x is handy for picking out the sign and flags from the kerb.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the booth on one of the vertical lines so the sign stays readable, and tap the sign so it's sharp. If the sky is bright, slide it a little darker so the flags keep their colour.
card.best_time: Early morning is best, when the crowds and traffic are lighter. Whenever you go, take a few shots in a row, because people and cars keep wandering through.
card.selfie_here: The small island with the sandbags is the classic backdrop. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the replica guardhouse over your shoulder. For the famous pose, one foot on each side of the old border, look for the red-and-white double row of stones across the intersection, and only do it when it's safe.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the hut, away from the queue, so both the US booth and the former East German booth area fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a busy junction with cars moving all the time, so shoot from the pavement and never step into the road for a better angle. Watch for pickpockets in the crowds. Costumed actors sometimes pose with visitors, so ask first if you want a photo with them.
card.challenge: Get the booth and its sign clear of people, then take a second shot where a few passers-by add a sense of scale. Which one do you like more?
card.good_to_know: The name comes from the letter C in the NATO phonetic alphabet. In October 1961, ten Soviet and ten American tanks faced each other near here, and the stand-off ended peacefully on 28 October. The guardhouse you see now is a replica. The metal container that replaced the original wooden shed in 1976 is at the Allied Museum in Dahlem.

card.hook: At street level the border is a puzzle. From the top of the viewing tower it clicks into place: two wall lines, a patrol road and a watchtower, all in one frame, with the TV Tower on the skyline.
card.stand_here: Head up the rooftop viewing tower at the Dokumentationszentrum Berliner Mauer, Bernauer Straße 111, opposite the preserved strip. Face the strip and look straight down. The main memorial point lies just to the south.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole strip. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the watchtower or the TV Tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the patrol road with one grid line so both wall lines run cleanly through the frame. If the sky is bright, tap the strip and drag darker a touch so the ground keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Soft, even light works best, so a bright overcast day is ideal for the view down onto the strip. The viewing tower has set opening days, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement on the strip side of Bernauer Straße, opposite the Documentation Centre, so the preserved strip and watchtower sit behind you. Use the front camera and try zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, to fit more of the scene over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the Documentation Centre side of the street (Bernauer Straße 111) and stand across the road, so the walls and watchtower show up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The preserved section is closed off, so you look at it from outside. Photos are fine here, but keep them respectful and skip staged or playful poses.
card.challenge: Can you get the patrol road dead straight on a grid line with the TV Tower still on the skyline? Take your time, it's a trickier balance than it sounds.
card.good_to_know: The memorial was created in 1998 to remember the division of Berlin and the people who died at the Wall. The 60-metre border section is kept as it was when the Wall fell. The oval Chapel of Reconciliation replaced a church destroyed in 1985 because it stood inside the border strip.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up the rooftop viewing tower at the Dokumentationszentrum Berliner Mauer, Bernauer Straße 111, opposite the preserved strip. Face the strip and look straight down. The main memorial point lies just to the south.

card.hook: Stand at this corner and the slabs look like a calm grey grid. Walk in and the ground dips, and the rows rise around you until the city goes quiet.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Ebertstraße and Behrenstraße, the northwest corner of the memorial. It's one block south of the Brandenburg Gate. Face south-east, so the grey field stretches away from you with the edge of the memorial close in front.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to get the whole edge of the field and the rows running away. Switch to 1x for a more natural look. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single row of slabs.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the edge of the nearest slabs up with them, so the rows look straight.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest, with fewer tour groups and school classes at the corner. The low sun also falls onto the blocks then, which makes the concrete look great.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, go inside the field. One traveller took theirs on the southwest side, after walking in from the Wilhelmstraße side and right through the blocks. Use the front camera at arm's length, keep the slabs framing you, and try a bright top so you stand out against the grey.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the southern edge of the field while you stand among the slabs, then check the framing together because there's no fixed spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Climbing on the stelae is discouraged and staff will ask you to get down, so keep your shots calm and respectful.
card.challenge: Find a narrow alley between the slabs and take one quiet shot with the rows running away to a single point.
card.good_to_know: The memorial was designed by architect Peter Eisenman with Buro Happold. It has 2,711 grey concrete slabs across 1.9 hectares, and their heights run from 0.2 metres to 4.7 metres. It was finished in December 2004 and opened to the public in May 2005. The open-air field is free to enter at any hour. For the underground information centre, check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Ebertstraße and Behrenstraße, the northwest corner of the memorial. It's one block south of the Brandenburg Gate. Face south-east, so the grey field stretches away from you with the edge of the memorial close in front.

selfie_spots.why: One travel blogger's photo was taken from inside the field, with the blocks framing the shot, and the blogger recommends walking through the memorial rather than stopping at the edge.

card.hook: The World Clock does half your work here: one glance at your photo and everyone knows it's Berlin, with the TV Tower shooting up behind it. Just expect a few strangers to wander through, because this is reputedly the most visited part of the city.
card.stand_here: Stand in Alexanderplatz near the World Clock (Weltzeituhr) and face across the square toward the TV Tower. The Fountain of the Peoples' Friendship is about 1 minute on foot to the west if you want a second shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the tower with the clock in front. Switch to 0.5x to fit the whole square and the tower in one frame. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the top of the tower or details of the fountain.
card.make_it_pop: Turn the phone upright, switch on the gridlines, and put the World Clock on a lower line so the tower rises through the top of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the evening is likely to be quieter. A clear sky helps the tower stand out, so peek at the weather first.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the World Clock with the TV Tower behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in the whole tower, and hold the phone a bit low so the tower stays over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Alexanderplatz is an open public square. If you want to go up the TV Tower or visit anything else ticketed nearby, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the clock low, the tower tall, and no stranger crossing your shot. You'll need a few tries, because people keep walking through.
card.good_to_know: The square is named after Russian Tsar Alexander I, who was welcomed here on a parade ground in October 1805. King Frederick William III renamed it on 2 November 1805. Before that it lay just outside the city wall by the George Gate and served as a cattle market, then a major wool market.

card.hook: Most walls want you to look away, but this one is covered in colour and begs you to stare. Start where the paint meets the bridge and you'll get the Wall and the Oberbaum Bridge towers in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Mühlenstraße and Warschauer Straße, where the gallery begins at the bridge end. Face the painted wall so it fills the foreground, with the Oberbaum Bridge towers rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the wall and the bridge towers into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched view of a few murals together, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a single painting.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the top of the wall up with a grid line so it doesn't tilt, then tap the wall and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go on a weekday if you can, because weekend crowds can block the main shots. Whatever the day, take a few frames and let people walk out of the picture.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the 'Fraternal Kiss' mural on the riverside path, about halfway along the gallery, roughly 200 m to the left of the Mercedes Arena when facing the river. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it up so the mural fills the space behind your shoulder. If you're near the Ostbahnhof end, Birgit Kinder's Trabant mural breaking through the wall is another good backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at the corner of Mühlenstraße and Warschauer Straße, where the gallery begins. Stand with the wall behind you and ask them to step back until the whole stretch fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Some murals are sometimes covered during restoration work, so check the official site before you go. Parked cars along the road can block the view from the roadside, so pick your angle with care.
card.challenge: Find the Brezhnev and Honecker kiss, fill your whole frame with it, then take one more shot with your best 'I'm not jealous' face beside it.
card.good_to_know: The East Side Gallery is 1,316 metres of murals painted straight onto a surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall. In spring 1990, soon after the Wall opened, 118 artists from 21 countries painted it, commenting on the political changes of 1989 and 1990. It's now a protected heritage monument, and there's no paid entry.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Mühlenstraße and Warschauer Straße, where the gallery begins at the bridge end. Face the painted wall so it fills the foreground, with the Oberbaum Bridge towers rising behind it.

card.hook: Picture a huge green dome, a wide open lawn, and about a hundred other people trying to get the same shot as you. Berlin Cathedral is so symmetrical that it practically poses for you.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Lustgarten, right in front of the cathedral, with the cathedral to the north-east of you (about 2 minutes on foot from where you arrive). Face the dome head-on so the lawn and paving lead the eye up to it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and dome in, with plenty of lawn or paving in front. Switch to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for details of the dome and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or the dome, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the green dome (and wipe your phone's camera glass first, fingerprints love it).
card.best_time: The Lustgarten is busy through the day, so early morning or later in the evening should give you a clearer view. When you arrive, check how the light looks on the facade and tweak brighter or darker to suit.
card.selfie_here: Head for the Lustgarten lawn beside the fountain just in front of the cathedral's main facade. Reviewers say its central position lets you frame the cathedral behind you. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the dome over your shoulder. The fountain is seasonal, so it may look different, or be switched off, when you visit. For fewer photobombers, one guide likes the Friedrichsbrücke bridge over the Spree, where the cathedral is in view across the river.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand back on the central lawn near the fountain, facing the cathedral's symmetrical front, so the whole building fits in the frame while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide advises care when sitting on the high balustrade of the Friedrichsbrücke. The Lustgarten is a free open park, but going inside the cathedral or up to the dome may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Line up the middle of the dome with the centre gridline, then wait for a gap in the crowd. Or turn the crowd into a feature and let a few people show how big this place is.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral you see today went up between 1894 and 1905 for Emperor William II, to plans by Julius Raschdorff. It's the largest Protestant church in Germany and a major burial place of the Hohenzollern family. It was damaged in the Second World War, and the interior was restored by 2002.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Lustgarten, right in front of the cathedral, with the cathedral to the north-east of you (about 2 minutes on foot from where you arrive). Face the dome head-on so the lawn and paving lead the eye up to it.

card.hook: Potsdamer Platz looks like a glass-and-steel jungle by day, but wait for dark. The Sony Center roof lights up above the towers and suddenly your phone has a proper subject.
card.stand_here: Stand on Potsdamer Platz in front of the Sony Center, about 1 km south of the Brandenburg Gate and the Reichstag. Face the Sony Center and look up and across the square, and the middle of the square lies to the south of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the roof and the surrounding towers into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look at the buildings, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details of the roof or the tops of the towers.
card.make_it_pop: After dark, switch on night mode, tuck your elbows against your body, tap the brightest part of the roof, then drag the brightness down a little so the lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the Sony Center roof and the towers around it look their best. Daytime works too if you want a clear view of the whole square.
card.selfie_here: Try the open square beside the reconstructed traffic signal tower, which a visitor guide lists as a good photo stop. Use your front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the tower over your shoulder; the Sony Center's covered courtyard under the roof is another option, but check on the spot what shows up behind you.
card.ask_someone: For a wider shot with you in it, you could try the traffic island in the middle of Leipziger Platz, a short walk from Potsdamer Platz, and ask a passer-by to take it. Check the view works once you're there.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is an open public space. For the Panoramapunkt or the Reichstag dome, check the official site before you go, as booking may be needed.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with them so the buildings stand up straight, then let the glowing roof fill the top of the frame with a little pavement below for scale.
card.good_to_know: The square is named after Potsdam, about 25 km to the south west, because the old road from Potsdam passed through Berlin's city wall here at the Potsdam Gate. It grew into one of the busiest junctions in Europe, was destroyed in the Second World War, and later the Berlin Wall ran straight through it. Most of the glass-and-steel buildings you see today date from the redevelopment after 1990.

card.hook: Here's a Berlin surprise: the famous silver-sphere TV Tower looks best when it's peeking out from behind a very old church. Traffic rumbles past, the Marienkirche spire points up, and the tower slips in right behind its cross.
card.stand_here: Stand on Karl-Liebknecht-Straße, on the stretch near the Marienkirche, and face south-east. The tower is to the south-east of you, rising behind the cross and spire of the church with the street's traffic in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower, the church spire and the street in one go. Switch to 1x for a calmer picture, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the tower and the church cross closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn your phone upright, switch on the gridlines, and put the church cross on one side and the tower's shaft on the other, with the sphere in the upper part of the frame.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sky has some colour or clouds, because a plain white sky makes the tower hard to pick out. Early in the day usually means fewer people on the pavement.
card.selfie_here: Head to the open ground beside Rathausstraße at the Marx-Engels-Forum, which a local photography guide recommends for full-length portraits. Stand with the tower rising directly behind you, face the front camera, and hold it low so the whole tower fits over your shoulder. If you'd rather have some history behind you, the columned walkway beside the Alte Nationalgalerie on Museum Island also has the tower in the backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back in the open square at Alexanderplatz while you stand in front of them with the tower behind you, and suggest zoom 0.5x so the full structure fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement and wait for a gap in the traffic if you want a cleaner foreground. The Marienkirche is closed to visitors during services, and the tower's visitor platform may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the church cross and the tower's sphere in the same frame, with the tower standing straight and not leaning?
card.good_to_know: East Germany's government built the tower between 1965 and 1969 as a broadcasting mast and a statement of power. At 368 metres including the antenna, it's the tallest structure in Germany. The visitor platform is about 203 metres up in the sphere, and the tower often shows up as the opening shot in films set in Berlin.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Karl-Liebknecht-Straße, on the stretch near the Marienkirche, and face south-east. The tower is to the south-east of you, rising behind the cross and spire of the church with the street's traffic in front.

card.hook: Picture a wide green lawn, a fountain, a row of tall stone columns and a big dome, all in one shot. That's the Lustgarten view of Museum Island, and it's the easiest win on the whole island.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Lustgarten, on the south-west side of the Altes Museum, and face the Berliner Dom. You'll see the columned museum and the dome together, with the lawn and fountain in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the Altes Museum and the Berliner Dom together. Go to 0.5x if you want the whole colonnade, the fountain and the dome in one frame. Try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for close-ups of the dome or the columns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the colonnade up with a horizontal line so the columns stay straight, then put the fountain or a strip of lawn in the bottom third.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and fewer people around the fountain. Midday sun can make the pale stonework look flat and bright.
card.selfie_here: Cross Friedrichsbrücke onto the island and turn right into the colonnade next to the Old National Gallery. Use the front camera and stand between the stone columns so they make an arch around you, and the TV Tower may peek out behind you from some spots.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Monbijou Park across the Spree, while you pose with the Bode Museum's dome behind you so it fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are banned on Museum Island, so use your arm. Bags over 30 x 20 x 10 cm have to go in a cloakroom or locker if you head inside a museum.
card.challenge: Get one photo where the columns are dead straight and the fountain is in the bottom third, then see if your travel buddy can spot the dome without help.
card.good_to_know: Most of Museum Island was built between 1830 and 1930, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. The Altes Museum is the oldest on the island and opened in 1830, designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel. The Pergamon Museum is closed for major renovation, so its facade may be covered by scaffolding.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Lustgarten, on the south-west side of the Altes Museum, and face the Berliner Dom. You'll see the columned museum and the dome together, with the lawn and fountain in front of you.

card.hook: Picture two long rows of linden trees marching toward a giant stone gate, with everyone else shooting from the middle of the square. You can do better than that, and it takes about three steps.
card.stand_here: Stand in Pariser Platz, a little back from the Brandenburg Gate on the Unter den Linden side, not in the middle of the square. Then turn east, toward the part of the avenue marked on the map, for the long view down the trees.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the gate and the trees together. If the crowds stop you stepping back, try 0.5x. Zoom 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) squeezes the tree lines together along the avenue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the gate's sides straight, then tap the gate and drag the brightness slider a little darker at sunset so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or around sunset, before the tour groups arrive. In winter the Christmas lights along the boulevard are a nice bonus.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and hold your phone a bit higher than usual. Keep the landmark over your shoulder and step to the side of the crowd so you both fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site for events or closures before you go.
card.challenge: Find a tree trunk or a streetlight and use it to frame your shot, then take the same picture at 1x and 2x and see which one you like more.
card.good_to_know: The linden trees you see today were replanted in the 1950s, after most of the earlier ones were lost in the 1930s and the last days of the war. The Zeughaus, built 1695-1706, is the oldest building on the street, and Schinkel's Neue Wache dates from 1817. Frederick the Great's statue on horseback has stood on the central strip since 1851.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Pariser Platz, a little back from the Brandenburg Gate on the Unter den Linden side, not in the middle of the square. Then turn east, toward the part of the avenue marked on the map, for the long view down the trees.

card.hook: Gendarmenmarkt looks like somebody drew it with a ruler: two matching domed towers, a grand concert hall and a poet standing in the middle. Even your wonkiest photo will look tidy here.
card.stand_here: Stand on the central steps of the Konzerthaus Berlin and face north toward the French Cathedral (Französischer Dom). The Schiller statue is a little to your right, towards the north-east, and the German Cathedral is behind you to the south.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the steps, the lion statue and the French Cathedral's tower into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer view, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the dome.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the French Cathedral on the centre line with the lion statue and steps below it, and keep your phone level so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or dusk usually gives softer light and lit-up buildings. Early in the day tends to be quieter on the steps. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against a railing or your body.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Konzerthaus steps with the building behind you and the square in view, using the front camera (and 0.5x if your phone offers it). For a classic souvenir, stand next to the Schiller monument in the middle of the square.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Konzerthaus steps beside the lion statue while you pose in the square in front of the steps, so they can fit the whole ensemble behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the churches can vary: non-flash photography for personal use is generally allowed, but check the signs or ask staff. A visitor tip also warns to watch out for thieves, so keep your phone and bag close. The French Cathedral's viewing platform is ticketed, and events can change access, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Line up the lion statue so it looks like it's guarding the French Cathedral's dome, then see whether you can get the same shot with no strangers in it.
card.good_to_know: The square dates from the end of the seventeenth century and was reconstructed in 1773. The Huguenot community built the French Cathedral between 1701 and 1705, and Karl Friedrich Schinkel designed the Konzerthaus in 1821. Most of the buildings were badly damaged or destroyed in the Second World War, and all have since been restored. The Christmas market fills the square and steps, so expect a very different scene at that time of year.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the central steps of the Konzerthaus Berlin and face north toward the French Cathedral (Französischer Dom). The Schiller statue is a little to your right, towards the north-east, and the German Cathedral is behind you to the south.

card.hook: The Humboldt Forum's stone front is so long and so formal that it can feel like it's daring you to fit it in one photo. Good news: the Lustgarten gives you the room to do it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Lustgarten, near the Altes Museum, and face the north facade of the Humboldt Forum. Step back across the lawn and paving until the whole front fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole north front and the open square, then try 1x for a more natural look. Zoom 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) picks out Portal V and the Sanchi gate replica.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the facade up with the horizontal lines and hold your phone level, so the walls stay straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Soft, even daylight suits the stone front, and early morning is likely to be quieter in the square. An overcast sky gives flatter light, but it's nice and even.
card.selfie_here: Try the Schlossplatz square in front of the Humboldt Forum: use the front camera and keep the facade over your shoulder. The Schlüterhof courtyard is another option, with the baroque facade behind you and café tables around.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are not permitted over Museum Island. Check the official site before you go to confirm whether the roof terrace is open and what photography is allowed inside.
card.challenge: Take your wide shot first, then zoom in and make the Sanchi gate replica the star of a second picture.
card.good_to_know: The Humboldt Forum is a museum of world cultures and art in the reconstructed Berlin Palace on Museum Island. It's named after the Prussian scholars Wilhelm and Alexander von Humboldt. It opened on 20 July 2021, and its last wing followed in September 2022. This ground-level view needs no ticket.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Lustgarten, near the Altes Museum, and face the north facade of the Humboldt Forum. Step back across the lawn and paving until the whole front fits.

The Rathausbrücke page is a cathedral photo guide, and no page confirms a spot showing the whole building in one frame; treat the ask-someone suggestion as approximate. The berlin.de and Berlinwalk pages describe the square and courtyard but do not say they are the best selfie spots, so the choices rest on those descriptions rather than an explicit recommendation.

card.hook: A gold lady stands alone in the middle of a busy Berlin roundabout, high above the traffic, and Berliners call her Goldelse. She glows against the sky and trees, so she's easy to love through a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Straße des 17. Juni, the tree-lined avenue west of the Großer Stern roundabout, and face east toward the column. From here the Brandenburg Gate lines up behind it. Stay on the pavement and out of the traffic.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x. If you want the Brandenburg Gate to look closer behind the column, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone. Save zoom 0.5x for the low shot from the tunnel stairs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the column on the middle vertical line with a little sky above Victoria, then tap the column and drag a touch darker so the gold keeps its detail.
card.best_time: A visitor guide recommends golden hour, when the light is soft and the gold glows. Arriving early also helps you beat the crowds.
card.selfie_here: Try the underpass steps behind Café Victoria at the Großer Stern: find the columned structure, go down the stairs and follow the underpass until just before it comes back up to ground level. It's a quieter spot, but the column ends up in front of you rather than behind you, so we can't promise the classic over-the-shoulder shot. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your arm out.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the staircase that leads down a few steps from the column while you stand in front of the column, so its full height fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The column sits inside a busy roundabout, so shoot only from the pavements and pedestrian zones and take care near traffic.
card.challenge: Get Goldelse perfectly centred on the gridline with a little sky above her head, then see if you can snap the Brandenburg Gate behind her too.
card.good_to_know: The Victory Column opened on 2 September 1873 to mark Prussian victories and was designed by Heinrich Strack. It first stood on Königsplatz (now Platz der Republik) and was moved to the Großer Stern in 1938–39, when it was made taller. It reaches about 67 metres today. The viewing platform needs a ticket, and your photos from up there won't include the column itself.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Straße des 17. Juni, the tree-lined avenue west of the Großer Stern roundabout, and face east toward the column. From here the Brandenburg Gate lines up behind it. Stay on the pavement and out of the traffic.

selfie_spots.why: Coming up from the underpass gives a quiet, less crowded view of the column, though the column ends up in front of you rather than behind.

card.hook: From the pavement, Bebelplatz looks like a calm postcard: pale stone, big sky, and a copper dome. Then you walk out onto the cobbles and spot a glass panel that opens onto a room of empty white shelves.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement on the north side of Unter den Linden and face south across the square. The State Opera is on your left, St. Hedwig's Cathedral is centre-left, and the Old Library and Humboldt law school are on your right.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square in. Then switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the cathedral's dome and the opera facade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building edges with them so everything stands up straight.
card.best_time: Go early in the day for fewer people in your shot. Soft daylight suits the pale stone best.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the glass panel of the Empty Library memorial, near the middle of the square, with St. Hedwig's Cathedral behind you and Humboldt University on your right. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and keep it quick and respectful, because this is a memorial.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Unter den Linden pavement facing south while you stand out on the open cobbles in front of them, so the opera and the cathedral frame you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral has been under renovation, so check whether its exterior is accessible before you plan a shot around it. If you want to go inside the cathedral or opera house, check their official sites first.
card.challenge: Get the full set of three: one wide shot of the square, one straight down through the glass at the white shelves, and one of the dome. Do it without a single stranger in the frame.
card.good_to_know: The square was laid out between 1741 and 1743 under Frederick II of Prussia, and the buildings were restored in the 1950s after wartime damage. On 10 May 1933, around 20,000 books were burned here in a Nazi ceremony. Micha Ullman's Empty Library marks the spot, and the white shelves below the glass are big enough to hold every one of those books.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement on the north side of Unter den Linden and face south across the square. The State Opera is on your left, St. Hedwig's Cathedral is centre-left, and the Old Library and Humboldt law school are on your right.

selfie_spots.why: It puts the square's best-known feature under your feet and frames the cathedral behind you.

card.hook: Picture a little red-brick city gate that wandered into the middle of the river, with a U-Bahn train rattling across the top. That's the Oberbaum Bridge, and it's a lot more photogenic than most bridges.
card.stand_here: Stand on the small outcrop on the Friedrichshain riverbank, on Mühlenstraße between the bridge and the Wall Museum, right beside the East Side Gallery. Face south-west, with the Spree in front of you and the bridge ahead.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get both towers, the bridge and the river in one frame. Try 0.5x for more water and sky in front, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the towers and arches.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the brick doesn't turn into a dark shape.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening works best, when the sun is low behind the bridge. The golden hour before sunset and the blue hour just after are both lovely. After sunset, switch on night mode and keep your elbows tucked in to hold the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Spree riverbank just west of the bridge, facing away from the water so the bridge is over your shoulder. The Kreuzberg bank near Schlesische Straße is another popular photo spot. Use the front camera (or 0.5x to fit more bridge in), and check the framing before you settle in, as the bridge may sit a bit off to one side.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the small outcrop between the bridge and the Wall Museum and ask a passer-by to take your photo with the bridge and towers behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography at the bridge is generally allowed, but commercial photography may need permits, so be kind about other people's privacy. The bridge carries road traffic, cyclists and trains, so stay on the bank and well away from the roadway and tracks.
card.challenge: Turn on Live Photos and catch a U-Bahn train crossing the upper deck between the two towers.
card.good_to_know: The bridge was finished in 1896. Designer Otto Stahn gave it a North German Brick Gothic look, like a small city gate, with pointed arches, coats of arms and two towers. The towers were modelled on a gate tower in Prenzlau and are just for show. After being damaged in the Second World War and sitting on the Berlin Wall border, it was rebuilt with a modern steel middle section by Santiago Calatrava and reopened on 9 November 1994.

card.hook: Picture a long red-brick giant with a clock tower in the middle, and a bronze Neptune lounging in front of it like he owns the place. That's the Rotes Rathaus, and it's very hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Walk to the Neptunbrunnen (the Neptune Fountain) in front of the building. It's a short walk from Alexanderplatz. Face the town hall so the fountain sits low in front of you and the tower rises behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the fountain, the whole width of the front and the tower in one frame. Try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the clock.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the tower on the middle vertical line and keep your phone level so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: The warm red brick really stands out against the sky, so pick a clear spell if you can. Check for roadworks before you go, whatever the hour, because they can block the fountain angles.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the stone benches by the Neptunbrunnen, on the side facing the town hall's front. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the brick facade and clock tower fit over your shoulder, with the fountain beside you. Double-check which way the benches face when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the fountain's edge facing the town hall while you stand by the fountain with the full building behind you, though construction in the square may limit where anyone can stand.
card.rules_and_safety: Pickpockets are reported in this busy area, so keep your phone strap and bag secure while you frame the shot. It's a working government building, so check the official site before you go if you want to head inside.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead centre on the gridline with Neptune low in the foreground, then see if you can count all 25 bays across the front.
card.good_to_know: Hermann Friedrich Waesemann designed the Rotes Rathaus in the Renaissance Revival style, and it was finished in 1869. It was badly damaged in the Second World War, rebuilt to the original plans, and reopened on 30 November 1955. Today it houses the Governing Mayor of Berlin and the Senate, and the clock was re-gilded in 2006.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the Neptunbrunnen (the Neptune Fountain) in front of the building. It's a short walk from Alexanderplatz. Face the town hall so the fountain sits low in front of you and the tower rises behind it.

card.hook: Most buildings on Unter den Linden shout for attention. The Neue Wache just stands there, flat-fronted and calm, daring you to get its columns straight.
card.stand_here: Stand on Unter den Linden, on the north side of the boulevard, opposite the Zeughaus. Face the building and you get the full front with its Doric columns and frieze, set a little back from the avenue. It's the classic postcard angle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front in one go. If people or traffic crowd you, drop to 0.5x, but keep the phone level so the columns don't lean. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) is great for the frieze and the column tops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the middle columns up with the centre of the frame, so the symmetry looks deliberate.
card.best_time: Daylight shows off the stone and the frieze best, and early in the day the pavement is usually quieter. Dusk is also worth a go with night mode, held steady against a lamp post or railing.
card.selfie_here: Go up the steps to the portico (Unter den Linden 4), turn to face the boulevard and use the front camera with the building behind you. If your front camera has a 0.5x button, try it to squeeze more of the columns in.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine inside, but be discreet and respectful, and keep the flash off, especially near the central sculpture. Check the official site for visiting arrangements and closures before you go in.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the columns line up so neatly your friends swear you used a ruler.
card.good_to_know: Karl Friedrich Schinkel designed the Neue Wache, and it was built between 1816 and 1818 as a guardhouse for the Royal Palace and a memorial to the Liberation Wars. Since 1993 it has been the Central Memorial of the Federal Republic of Germany to the Victims of War and Tyranny. Inside, Käthe Kollwitz's sculpture Mother with her Dead Son sits right under an open circular skylight.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Unter den Linden, on the north side of the boulevard, opposite the Zeughaus. Face the building and you get the full front with its Doric columns and frieze, set a little back from the avenue. It's the classic postcard angle.

card.hook: Picture a bombed-out church tower with a jagged top, and right beside it a wall of glowing blue glass. Berliners call the old tower "the hollow tooth", and it's even better in person.
card.stand_here: Head for Breitscheidplatz, where the church is about 1 minute on foot, to the west. Stand on the far side of the square and face the church, so the broken old tower and the modern blue-glass church fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the old tower, the new church and a bit of the square all squeeze in. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, and 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for the top of the ruined spire.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness darker a little so the sky and the blue glass keep their colour, and switch on gridlines to keep the tower standing straight.
card.best_time: Daytime is great for the blue glass and clear views of the ruin. In the evening the floodlit tower looks lovely from the square, so switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the open part of Breitscheidplatz facing the church, so the ruined tower and the blue new church are behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it up slightly to fit it all in. No guide names an exact selfie spot, so treat this as a good starting point and wander a little.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the open square, so the broken tower, the modern church and the bell tower all fit in while you stand in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, so if you go inside, keep the flash off and be considerate of anyone there to pray. The ruined tower may have limited access, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo of the "hollow tooth" and one of the blue glass, then see if you can line them up in a single frame without a stranger wandering through.
card.good_to_know: The old church was built in the 1890s and badly damaged in an air raid in 1943, and the ruin was kept on purpose. The modern buildings around it went up between 1959 and 1963, designed by Egon Eiermann. Their concrete honeycomb walls hold 21,292 pieces of mostly blue stained glass, and the old spire now stands about 71 metres high.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Breitscheidplatz, where the church is about 1 minute on foot, to the west. Stand on the far side of the square and face the church, so the broken old tower and the modern blue-glass church fit in one frame.
